course: NISM Series III-C: Securities Intermediaries Compliance (Fund)
overview: Imagine you want to buy a toll plaza on a national highway because it generates daily cash, but it costs ₹1,000 Crores. You can't buy it alone. This is where an Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT) comes in. An InvIT is like a mutual fund, but instead of buying stocks, it pools money from investors to buy massive infrastructure projects (like roads, power plants, and gas pipelines). For the NISM exam, this chapter explains the structure of InvITs, the strict rules on what they can buy (mostly completed projects), and their mandatory dividend payouts. As a Compliance Officer, you must ensure the trust doesn't take too much debt and distributes its profits fairly to the public.

complete_concept_explanation.concept: 1. The Four Pillars (Structure of an InvIT)
complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: An InvIT is set up as a Trust and is managed by four different parties to ensure safety, fairness, and efficiency.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Step 1: **The Sponsor**. This is the infrastructure developer (like a big construction company) who sets up the InvIT and transfers their infrastructure assets into it. 
Step 2: **The Trustee**. An independent SEBI-registered entity that legally holds the assets on behalf of the investors and watches over everyone else to prevent fraud. 
Step 3: **The Investment Manager**. The 'Financial Brain'. They decide which new highways or power plants to buy or sell, manage the debt, and handle the daily financial operations. 
Step 4: **The Project Manager**. The 'Physical Muscle'. They are physically on the ground, repairing the roads, collecting the tolls, and making sure the power plant is actually running.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam Importance: You must know the difference in the roles of the Investment Manager and Project Manager. Practical Importance: A Compliance Officer usually sits within the Investment Manager's office and must report compliance statuses to the Trustee.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: In the 'IRB InvIT Fund' (a popular toll-road InvIT), IRB Infrastructure Developers is the Sponsor. They built the roads, transferred them to the Trust, and now a separate Project Manager ensures the toll booths are working 24/7 so the investors get their money.
exam_traps: Confusing the Project Manager with the Investment Manager. Remember: Project Manager does the physical/operational work; Investment Manager does the financial/strategy work.
Thinking the Sponsor owns the assets forever. No, once transferred, the assets are held by the Trust (via the Trustee) for the benefit of the unitholders.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: S.T.I.P: Sponsor (Starts), Trustee (Tracks), Investment Manager (Invests), Project Manager (Physical work).

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: SEBI forces public InvITs to buy 'safe', completed projects that are already making money, rather than risky, under-construction ones.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation: Infrastructure projects are notorious for delays (land issues, court cases). To protect retail investors, SEBI mandates that a Publicly Listed InvIT must invest at least **80%** of the value of its assets in **completed and revenue-generating** infrastructure projects. A maximum of 20% can be invested in under-construction projects or other safe liquid instruments (like government bonds). If an InvIT wants to invest heavily (>10%) in under-construction projects, it is not allowed to take money from the general public; it must become a 'Privately Placed' InvIT for large institutional investors only.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam Importance: The 80% rule is heavily tested. Practical Importance: Compliance must vet every new asset purchase to ensure the 80% completed-asset limit is never breached.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Minimum Investment in Completed Projects = 80% of total asset value.
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: Out of every ₹100 the InvIT invests, at least ₹80 must go into projects that are fully built and actively earning money (like a working toll road).
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example: An InvIT has raised ₹1,000 Crores. It buys a fully working solar park for ₹850 Crores (85%) and puts ₹150 Crores (15%) into a solar park that is still being built. This is VALID because the completed project value (85%) is greater than the required 80%.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: India Grid Trust (IndiGrid) owns thousands of kilometers of working power transmission lines. They only buy lines that are already fully constructed and actively transmitting electricity, ensuring immediate cash flow for their investors.
exam_traps: Thinking public InvITs cannot buy under-construction projects at all. They can, but it is strictly capped at a maximum of 20% of their total value.
Confusing Public InvIT rules with Private InvIT rules. Private InvITs have much more freedom to invest in under-construction projects.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: 80% Done, 20% to Run. (80% must be completed).

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: InvITs cannot hoard the cash they earn; they must distribute almost all of it to the investors regularly.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation: [Image illustrating cash flow from an infrastructure project being distributed to unitholders of an InvIT] One of the biggest attractions of an InvIT is regular income. SEBI regulations state that an InvIT must distribute at least **90%** of its Net Distributable Cash Flows (NDCF) to the unit holders. For a publicly listed InvIT, this distribution must happen at least once every half-year (though many do it quarterly). The cash is usually distributed in three forms: Interest, Dividend, and Return of Capital.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam Importance: The '90%' figure and the 'half-yearly' frequency are guaranteed exam questions. Practical Importance: If the 90% distribution is missed, it is a severe regulatory violation that the Compliance Officer must answer for.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Distribution ≥ 90% of Net Distributable Cash Flows (NDCF).
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: Whatever pure cash profit the Trust makes after paying its operational bills and debt interest, it must give 90% of it back to the investors.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example: An InvIT collects ₹100 Crores in tolls. It pays ₹10 Crores for road maintenance and ₹10 Crores as interest to banks. The Net Distributable Cash Flow is ₹80 Crores. The InvIT MUST distribute at least ₹72 Crores (90% of 80) to its unitholders.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: If you buy 1,000 units of a Power Grid InvIT, you will notice that every 3 or 6 months, money automatically lands in your bank account. This is the InvIT complying with the 90% mandatory distribution rule.
exam_traps: Thinking the InvIT must distribute 90% of its 'Gross Revenue'. False! It is 90% of the *Net Distributable Cash Flow* (after expenses are paid).
Assuming distributions only happen once a year. For public InvITs, it must be at least half-yearly.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: InvITs are generous: They keep 10 and give you 90.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: A legal cap on how much debt the InvIT can take, ensuring it doesn't go bankrupt.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Infrastructure requires huge money, so InvITs often borrow from banks. However, SEBI sets strict limits to protect investors from excessive debt: 
1. **Base Limit**: The total consolidated borrowing of the InvIT cannot exceed **49%** of the value of its assets. 
2. **Enhanced Limit**: An InvIT can increase its borrowing up to **70%**, but ONLY if it meets three strict conditions: 
   - It must get a top-tier credit rating of **'AAA'**. 
   - It must get approval from **75%** of the unitholders by value. 
   - It must have a proven track record of at least 6 continuous distributions post-listing.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Exam Importance: Knowing both the 49% base limit and the 70% enhanced limit is crucial. Practical Importance: The Compliance Officer must certify the leverage ratio every quarter to ensure the fund hasn't borrowed too much.
complete_concept_explanation.formula:
Base Borrowing Limit ≤ 49% of Asset Value. 
Max Borrowing Limit (with AAA rating) ≤ 70% of Asset Value.
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: An InvIT cannot have more loans than equity, unless it proves it is incredibly safe (AAA rating), in which case it can borrow up to 70%.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example: An InvIT has total assets of ₹1,000 Crores. Under normal rules, it can only take a bank loan up to ₹490 Crores (49%). If it wants to borrow ₹600 Crores (60%), it must first get an 'AAA' rating and hold a vote where 75% of investors say 'Yes'.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: Many mature InvITs in India aim to keep their debt around 45% to stay safely below the 49% limit, so they don't have to go through the difficult process of getting an AAA rating and calling a massive unitholder vote.
exam_traps: Forgetting the exact conditions for the 70% limit (AAA rating + 75% unitholder approval).
Thinking the limit applies only to the Trust. It is a 'Consolidated' limit, meaning the debt of the Trust + the debt of the underlying projects (SPVs) combined.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Debt Limits: 49 is Fine. 70 needs an AAA (Triple A) and a 'Yay' (Approval).

important_differences.clear_explanation: 1. Underlying Assets: Mutual Funds buy paper (shares and bonds). InvITs buy physical infrastructure (highways, power lines). 2. Distributions: Mutual funds can choose to reinvest all profits (Growth plan). InvITs are legally forced to distribute 90% of their cash flows.

important_differences.difference_between: Publicly Listed InvIT vs Privately Placed InvIT
important_differences.clear_explanation: 1. Investors: Public InvITs are for everyone (retail minimum is ₹10,000 - ₹15,000). Private InvITs are for rich institutions (minimum investment is usually ₹1 Crore). 2. Investment Rules: Public InvITs must put 80% in completed projects. Private InvITs can invest heavily in under-construction projects.

frequently_asked_exam_areas: The requirement to invest a minimum of 80% in completed/revenue-generating assets.
The rule mandating the distribution of at least 90% of Net Distributable Cash Flows.
The specific roles of the Investment Manager vs the Project Manager.
The Base Leverage limit (49%) and the conditions for the Enhanced Leverage limit (70%).
quick_revision_summary: InvITs pool money to invest directly in infrastructure assets.
Structure: Sponsor, Trustee, Investment Manager, Project Manager.
Public InvITs: Min 80% in completed projects; max 20% in under-construction.
Must distribute 90% of net cash flows to unitholders at least half-yearly.
Base borrowing limit is 49% of asset value; can go to 70% with AAA rating and 75% approval.
Retail investors can easily buy public InvIT units on the stock exchange.
